item.title: Digital.Truth
item.description:
As part of our digital peacebuilding project, we offer workshops for parents and teachers on how to address misinformation and conspiracy theories.

Timeframe: 2023 - 2024

Due to the Corona pandemic, the war in Ukraine, economic crises or the advancing climate change, we find ourselves in a societal poly-crisis causing insecurity not only amongst young people, but also amongst adults. This, in turn, increases vulnerability to misinformation and conspiracy theories. By conveying simplified world views, conspiracy theories offer orientation and a sense of security. Furthermore, they provide a high identification potential, their spread has greatly increased throughout the Internet and social media and debunking conspiracy theories has proven to be extraordinarily difficult. Prevention is, therefore, crucial.

Parents, teachers and multipliers impart knowledge and competencies. They are an important source of information for young people – especially in times of crises. Parents and educators can accompany children and young people towards a confident and safe approach to media if they themselves have knowledge and skills about misinformation and conspiracy theories.

Our project "Digital.Truth" develops a workshop format that enables adults to recognise patterns of conspiracy theory narratives. They gain knowledge about the networks that feed misinformation and mistrust in government systems, as well as undermine democracies. "Digital.Truth" takes a transgenerational approach, training young adults as facilitators for the workshops. In this way, an exchange about the experiences of young people on the Internet and social media can take place amongst the participating parents and teachers.

Do you have questions about our work or would you like to participate in a workshop? Contact us directly email hidden; JavaScript is required.

Background

In their role as parents or multipliers (pedagogical staff), adults are confronted with the reasonable expectation to properly classify information and offer orientation. This is the case especially in times of crises. For a considerable number of adults, it is a challenge to recognise misinformation on the Internet.

As doubts about the independence of the press are spreading, it is important to strengthen adults' resilience to conspiracy theories and misinformation. If they are aware of the risks that conspiracy theories pose to societies, democracies and the private sphere, they can accompany young people in their everyday lives and guide them in a competent and safe use of the media. In this way, they can also become aware of the steps to take for a peaceful democratic coexistence.

Approach

On a scientific and pedagogical-didactical basis, "Digital.Truth" develops a workshop format on misinformation and conspiracy theories for adults - especially for parents and teachers. It will be suitable for implementation both in person and online.

The format addresses three themes by:

  1. Adressing motives and needs of conpsiracy theories together with the participants,
  2. Sharing knowledge and skills for identifying and deconstructing conspiracy theory narratives and misinformation, and
  3. Facilitating a space for intergenerational exchange about anti-democratic phenomena on the web.

The individual topics are modular and include innovative learning materials. Interactive methods allow a stimulating transfer of knowledge and skills in dealing with misinformation and conspiracy theories. The approach enables socio-emotional learning and strengthens the resilience and ambiguity tolerance of the participants.

Young adults are trained to conduct the workshops. The transgenerational approach offers an innovative exchange format for joint learning and a change of perspective. The workshops are tailored to the target groups and their needs.

Goals and Results

By the end of the project in 2024, 50 workshops aimed to be held throughout Germany, with at least 800 parents and 200 teachers aiming to be reached. Teachers nationwide will receive training that is easily accessible and tailored to their needs and 20 young adults will be trained as facilitators for the workshops.

The workshop materials will be available for educational staff to be downloaded free of charge.

The project is accompanied by a social media campaign.

Key Actors

Parents of all educational backgrounds, teachers from all disciplines and school types as well as pedagogical professionals can participate in the free workshops.

Young adults are trained as facilitators to conduct the workshops.

Partners and Funders

The project „Digital.Truth“ is funded by the Federal Ministry for Family Affairs, Senior Citizens, Women and Youth within the program “Demokratie leben!”.

In addition, the project is funded by Humanity in Action in 2023.

  • Tackling conspiracy thinking and disinformation through peace education 12 Dec 2024

item.title: National Dialogue and peacemaking
item.description:
This seven-week online course provides an in-depth understanding of National Dialogues and how to prepare, conduct and implement them.

Timeframe: 3 September 2026 - 15 October 2026

The course combines various learning formats, features leading experts and experienced practitioners, and immerses in real-world case studies.

The innovative course structure is comprised of three components in order to ensure a comprehensive learning experience:

  1. An e-learning tool with five self-paced course units,
  2. Five live facilitated peer-exchange sessions accompanying each unit,
  3. Five live sessions with input from leading experts and a Q&A following each peer-exchange session.

These elements build on one another so you can deepen the knowledge you gained in the self-paced learning units by exchanging with your peers and engaging in lively discussions with experts.

We will also discuss the nexus of National Dialogues and current topics such as climate change, protest movements, and digitalisation. You will also have the opportunity to present your own work on National Dialogues, whether to reflect on past experiences or brainstorm on the challenges of an ongoing process.

The course language is English.
Tuition fee: 1.750 EUR
Reduced tuition fee: 1.200 EUR

Applications for reduced tuition close 31 May 2026
General applications close 30 June 2026

Who should attend

This course is designed for individuals who are likely to participate in, contribute to the design of or provide support for a National Dialogue process. This includes:

  • National stakeholders from countries considering or initiating a National Dialogue process to deal with a deep political crisis or political transition,
  • Professionals from the diplomatic field, policy sector or peacebuilding organisations who are supporting or may support a National Dialogue process,
  • Academics, practitioners and the peacebuilding community at large who would like to learn about National Dialogues and how they might contribute to conflict transformation.

Learning objectives

This course offers the opportunity to expand your knowledge on both the theoretical and practical levels. This includes:

  • Establishing a joint understanding of the purpose, key features and phases of National Dialogues,
  • Situating National Dialogue in the broader conflict transformation landscape and how it links to other processes,
  • Taking a closer look at some of the most critical aspects of National Dialogues such as agenda setting and mandate, inclusivity and ownership, participation and power dynamics, process design, implementation structures and follow-up mechanisms,
  • Reflecting on common challenges and dilemmas and drawing lessons from past National Dialogue processes,
  • Covering certain under-explored nexus areas and how to best integrate those topics in the design of National Dialogues,
  • Bridging theory and practice through live expert sessions and real-world case studies,
  • Contextualising the various aspects of National Dialogues to your own context for deep practical insights,
  • Becoming part of a global community of practice through exchanging and learning alongside peers from around the world.

Why the Berghof Foundation?

The Berghof Foundation has over 50 years of experience in supporting conflict transformation processes around the world, including peace mediation and National Dialogue support. We have worked extensively on supporting National Dialogue processes in various countries such as Lebanon, Yemen, Sudan, South Sudan and Ethiopia. In 2017, we published the National Dialogue Handbook: A Guide for Practitioners in collaboration with swisspeace. This Handbook is the most comprehensive publication on the topic and includes 19 cases studies. We have also developed and conducted many courses, trainings and workshops on National Dialogue, working with national actors, international organisations, ministries and academics. Drawing on this extensive experience, the course has been designed to provide participants with a theoretical framework and immerse them in real-world examples of National Dialogues.

Methodology

This online course combines various learning formats and components to provide you an enriching opportunity to learn, exchange and become part of a global community of practice.

You will have a weekly unit assignment in our interactive e-learning tool that you can complete on your own time and pace. After each unit assignment, you will join a facilitated live peer exchange session online to discuss any open questions and deepen your understanding through structured group discussions, exercises and reflections. These facilitated peer exchange sessions will help you establish a solid understanding of the subject matter and its nuances and you will benefit from the perspectives and experiences of fellow participants from around the world. You will also have the opportunity to engage in a live expert session with leading international experts and practitioners, which will include inputs from our experts, case studies from different conflict contexts and Q&As. During these sessions, you will be able to connect the theoretical knowledge you gained before with practical experiences and examples from our experts.

To apply for the course, please complete the application form and upload your CV.

General applications close 30 June 2026

Tuition Fee

Special consideration is given to Master’s or PhD students, unemployed individuals, or those working in grassroots NGOs in related fields, who can demonstrate financial need and the practical impact of the course. item.title: Insider mediators help resolve violent conflicts between miners and farmers in Zimbabwe
item.description:
Read Allanviny Murozvi and Billian Matambo’s story!

While farming has always been the backbone of the Zimbabwean economy, especially in rural communities, the country is also rich in much sought-after raw materials like platinum, chrome, or coal. Therefore, in many regions, farmers and miners compete for the use of land, which leads to conflict and can even escalate into intimidation or severe physical violence. In addition, conflicting legislation on mining, agriculture and environmental protection creates uncertainty and encourages arbitrary decision-making across these sectors, which not only causes conflict among institutions, but also exacerbates conflicts between farmers and miners on the ground.

In Chiadzwa, a ward in the Mutare District in eastern Zimbabwe, these conflicts were escalating when a national mining company and artisanal miners started forcing farmers out from their land, using state security actors to enforce these actions. But also farmers and pastoralists who had not been forcibly removed suffered from the mining activities. Often, their livestock was in danger of falling into unclosed mining holes or getting poisoned by the mines’ dumping sites. The intense mining activity in the region also had degraded soil fertility and led to farmers and miners competing for water access.

Two insider mediators from our network, Allanviny Murozvi and Billian Matambo, decided to start a mediation intervention to prevent the conflicts from escalating further and to help the miners and farmers find a mutual agreement. To do so, they brought together representatives from the conflicting parties, traditional leaders, policymakers, security agencies, and party officials for a mediation and dialogue process. At the dialogue meetings, the conflicting parties spoke directly with each other for the first time.

The communication workshop with its active listening components was the most useful aspect of our training. [W]e could apply it in our mediation interventions in a way that made all sides feel heard[…].

Before starting the process, Allanviny and Billian had taken part in the mediation and dialogue training that we co-organise with Africa University where they had learned about active listening methods. They applied these techniques during the mediation process and were able to help the conflict parties better understand the root causes of their conflict. “The communication workshop with its active listening components was the most useful aspect of our training. [W]e could apply it in our mediation interventions in a way that made all sides feel heard and solutions were more easily found because of it”, Allanviny and Billian told us.

Through the dialogues that the insider mediators facilitated, the farmers and miners saw that besides the conflicts over the use of land and environmental degradation, they both suffered from a high unemployment rate and had difficulties sustaining their livelihoods. With the insider mediator’s support, they agreed on how to share water resources sustainably. The local communities agreed to let the mining companies operate, as long as they agreed to reserve a set percentage of jobs for locals and committed to empowering and training local youth through scholarship programmes and traineeships. The mining company committed to redistributing a significant portion of its profits to the local community.

Allanviny and Billian’s mediation intervention laid the ground for community-driven solutions to resolve local disputes between the farmers and miners in Chiadzwa.

item.title: How communities are building climate resilience through shared water governance in Balad, Iraq

In the sub-district of Hatamiyah, Salah al-Din governorate, north of Baghdad, climate change is no longer an abstract concept. Shrinking water supplies and increasinlgy unpredictable water allocations are reshaping the lives of farming communities. These challenges are linked to declining water levels, shifting river channels, and irregular upstream releases in the Tigris River, ageing and inefficient secondary canals, limited electricity for irrigation pumps, irregular rainfall, and changing agricultural patterns, including reduced harvests and declining crop yields.

Newly emerged river-adjacent lands create disputes between landholders and farmers whose previously cultivated lands now lie farther from the river. This includes tensions over installing pumps, land concessions, and passage through private agricultural spaces as well as increasing tensions across tribal lines. Left unaddressed, these dynamics risk escalating into wider disputes, weakening social cohesion and undermining community resilience.

Our engagement in Balad started with a simple premise: Listen first

Berghof Foundation and Peace Paradigms Organisation convened and facilitated structured dialogue sessions that brought together community representatives, tribal leaders, and government officials to reflect on how climate-related pressures were affecting their daily lives. By providing a safe and inclusive space for exchange, participants developed a shared understanding and engaged in collective problem-solving. Building on individual experiences, participants explored how water scarcity had become a shared challenge requiring a collective response.

At first, participants simply exchanged their experiences and perspectives, listening to one another’s daily struggles. Through sustained engagement, trust was gradually built and space was created for all voices to be heard despite differing interests and internal tensions.

Our lands are dry – there is no water, and we don’t know what to do. No one is even willing to buy the lands because water cannot reach them.Participant of the dialogue sessions in Balad

Gradually, the conversations shifted towards exploring the challenges they all faced together, uncovering how water shortages had become a common problem. By the end of the dialogue sessions, which spanned seven months, the group had moved from discussion to action, collectively deciding to activate a Water Users Association (WUA) as a legal platform for collaborative water governance and conflict prevention. It was adopted by tribal leaders, community representatives, and local authorities as a solution to a community-wide problem.

Water User Associations (WUAs) are legal platforms that are governed by bylaws, which must be adhered to in order to receive official support from government institutions. They are registered under the Ministry of Water Resources. Members consist of farmers who are willing to join, own a plot of land irrigated from the designated water source, and have a renewed contract with the agriculture department.

Building a local institution for shared water management

In July 2025, WUA board elections marked a major milestone. Representatives from certain irrigation canals were elected to form a 22-person board that represents 975 WUA members. What emerged was not just a new organisational structure, but a functioning institution with real authority and clear responsibilities: managing water distribution, mediating disputes, strengthening participatory decision-making, and building trust across communities.

The WUA now supports fair allocation of water, maintains a comprehensive farmer database, and introduces new tools for conflict resolution. For many in Balad, this marks a fundamental shift away from fragmented and informal responses towards a coordinated, transparent approach grounded in shared responsibility.

Inclusion across tribal lines

Hatamiyah is shaped by strong tribal dynamics, including long-standing inequalities between larger tribes like the Tamim tribe and historically marginalised groups such as the Qareh Gol tribe. From the outset, the WUA was designed with these inequalities in mind: an inclusive coordination mechanism that ensures participation across tribal groups, as members from these groups are now part of the WUA and its elected board. Including the Qareh Gol tribe in the dialogue process and establishment of the WUA has been particularly significant as it gives them an active role in shaping water governance, strengthens their relationships with other communities and tribes, and helps reduce historical fragmentation and marginalisation.

Field observations indicate that the WUA has helped reduce inter-tribal tensions, broaden participation in local decision-making, and foster collective ownership over water management challenges. By creating a neutral space for dialogue and cooperation, the WUA has contributed to rebuilding trust and strengthening social cohesion in a community facing additional strain from climate change.

Opening space for youth and women

The WUA has also become a platform for gradual social change. While traditional structures in Balad have historically limited the participation of youth and women, their inclusion in the dialogue process marks an important first step towards more inclusive governance.

Women’s leadership is beginning to gain visibility. A woman official from the Balad Water Resources Department led the WUA election process within the tribal guesthouse, traditionally used for hospitality, mediation, and community decision-making, signalling growing acceptance of women in public leadership roles. These shifts are still at an early stage and will require sustained engagement, but they signal that norms are evolving around participation and representation.

Looking ahead: a model for climate-sensitive governance

The establishment of Iraq’s largest Water Users Association in terms of participants and water users marks a broader transition from informal, traditional conflict resolution mechanisms towards structured and institutionalised governance. Close collaboration between the WUA and officials from the Ministry of Water Resources at both provincial and national levels helped overcome registration challenges and strengthened links between community-based initiatives and public institutions.

Today, the WUA in Balad stands as a living example of how tribal, legal, and governance frameworks can align to address climate security risks. It offers a locally driven model for managing scarce resources, preventing conflict, and building resilience. This can inform future policy engagement and replication in other climate-affected areas in Iraq.

What began as a response to water scarcity has grown into something larger: a shared process of cooperation, participation, and trust-building. It shows what communities can achieve when they are supported with inclusive structures and dialogue. They can transform climate pressure into collective action.

item.title: Navigating climate and conflict
item.description:
Iraq is highly vulnerable to climate and environmental pressures, including water scarcity, soil degradation, extreme heat and increasingly frequent and intense dust storms. These pressures can deepen existing tensions, disrupt livelihoods and essential services, and increase the risk of conflict and displacement, particularly in areas affected by weak governance, socio-economic marginalisation and unresolved grievances. Against this backdrop, the Berghof Foundation and Peace Paradigms Organisation have worked from 2022 to 2026 to strengthen understanding of the climate-conflict nexus, support inclusive dialogue and mediation, and help Iraqi authorities integrate climate-security and conflict-sensitivity considerations into planning and decision-making. The report presents key outcomes, lessons learned and best practices.

item.title: Video: Building peace from the ground up
item.description:
Watch the recording of our International Day of Peace event to hear from peacebuilders about their day-to-day efforts in building lasting peace.

Peace is not achieved through a single agreement. It is built over time through the incremental efforts of peacebuilders that often remain invisible. To mark this year’s International Day of Peace, we shed light on the vital work of peacebuilders who lay the foundations for lasting peace.

The event brought together policymakers and practitioners to explore what it takes to build sustainable peace before, during, and after formal agreements. Drawing on experiences from Catalonia and Uganda among others, our speakers shared their stories on rebuilding trust where it has been eroded and on maintaining political and diplomatic momentum when progress is slow and setbacks are inevitable. They highlighted challenges and opportunities they encoutered along the way. The event also explored how the international community can recognise and invest more effectively in the everyday work required to turn peace agreements into lasting peace.

Watch the recording to hear from those working at the forefront of peacebuilding and learn how they enable societies to move from conflict to stability, reconciliation, and lasting peace.

item.title: International Day of Peace 2026: The small steps that make peace possible
item.description:
This International Day of Peace, voices from Uganda, Catalonia, and Colombia reveal how trust, dialogue, and persistence lay the groundwork for lasting peace.

Every year on 21 September, the United Nations marks the International Day of Peace, bringing people around the world together to reflect on the importance of building and sustaining peace. This year’s theme, “Invest in Peace: For Everyone, Everywhere, Every Day”, highlights the importance of investing in the people and processes that make peace possible. It highlights the role of the “everyday architects of peace”, the people who build relationships, bridge divides and lay the foundations for lasting peace within their communities.

This refelcts the reality of peace processes. Peace is rarely achieved through a single agreement or one defining moment. It is the process leading to it, and the work that follows, that determines whether peace can endure. Behind every agreement are countless interactions and decisions that rarely make the headlines: a meeting in which someone chooses to listen, a channel of communication that remains open during a crisis, or a trusted individual who can engage people across divides. These incremental advances can, over time, create the conditions for formal negotiations and agreements to take place.

This is where insider mediators can play a crucial role. Embedded within the societies and contexts affected by conflict, they bring a deep understanding of local relationships, dynamics and concerns. Their proximity and credibility enable them to engage with actors and communities who may be difficult for external mediators to reach, helping to build trust, open channels of communication and create opportunities for dialogue. Much of this work takes place away from the spotlight, yet it can be essential to sustaining communication and creating the conditions for progress.

As part of this year’s International Day of Peace campaign, mediators and peacebuilders from Uganda, Catalonia, and Colombia reflect on their experiences of peace processes and the steps that preceded formal agreements. Their experiences highlight the importance of the less visible stages of peace processes, including the conversations, compromises and acts of persistence that gradually build the confidence needed for progress.

Monsignor Hector Fabio Henao, Delegate for Church-State Relations of the Colombian Bishops’ Conference, played an important role in Colombia’s peace process and discusses the importance of working directly with local actors affected by conflict, building trust through dialogue, and recognising that meaningful peace takes time.

Stella Sabiiti is an Ugandan peacebuilder and mediator. She reflects on her role in insider mediation, where trusted relationships and a deep understanding of the parties can create space for dialogue and help overcome obstacles.

Former President of Catalonia Pere Aragones addresses the importance of being realistic about demands, celebrating small wins along the way and maintaining confidence throughout the process.

Our Executive Director Chris Coulter highlights that while signing an agreement marks an important transition, its lasting impact depends on what happens next, from putting commitments into practice to maintaining dialogue.

item.title: Rethinking local governance in Yemen
item.description:
Improved central-local relations are crucial for any future peace process in Yemen.

Under the slogan “take your mattress to the street”, citizens of Aden were sleeping in the middle of the road this summer. Others blocked strategic routes by burning tyres to protest the lack of electricity. In the past months, residents were lucky when they got two hours of electricity a day in the unbearable summer heat.

Electricity is not their only concern: water networks, sewage systems, street cleaning, and garbage collection are also not consistently available in Aden and beyond. As basic services remain often unreliable, Yemeni citizens’ frustration is growing.

Since taking office in February, the new government has taken several measures to address the situation. It has sought to streamline governance and security by placing them under one leadership in areas under its control, while promising to improve living conditions. It has also driven important economic reforms aimed at enhancing the economic and financial situation.

Overlapping competencies of local and central authorities

While these efforts may show results in the medium term, in the short term, local authorities continue to step in where the central government has been unable to provide. Often with support of international donors, and in some cases the Yemeni private sector, they have pursued ad hoc fixes for the most pressing local needs: rehabilitating water networks, renovating schools, and building or upgrading health centres. At the same time, local authorities have come up with economic development plans for their governorate, which outline their needs and opportunities, demonstrating their ambition and capacity to govern responsibly.

Unfortunately, these parallel efforts at central and local levels are sometimes in tension. Governorates with their own natural resources, such as Hadhramawt or Marib, have retained some or all their revenues rather than transferring them to the central level, allowing them to cover their substantial needs, while prompting criticism from the cash-strapped central government. Other governorates complain that budget allocations they are supposed to be receiving from the central government have not been received in years. In recent weeks, disputes have also emerged in Aden and Lahj over political appointments and which level of government has the authority to make them.

Rather than acting as partners in the country’s development, the two levels have increasingly become competitors for power and resources. Competencies are disputed and while the state pushes for greater oversight and control of funds, governorates complain that they are not receiving the support they need.

Need for constructive dialogue and cooperation

More dialogue between central and local levels is essential. Meetings between governors and the Ministry of Local Administration, for example, take place only when funding is available and, at best, once a year.

There is also a need to agree on the rules of the game. Should the government strive to restore the level of centralisation that existed prior to the outbreak of the war, more than a decade ago? Would governorates agree? Should Local Authority Law No. 4 of 2000 be fully implemented, with laws and practices that contravene it being eliminated? Or should more of the de facto arrangements that have emerged in the last few years be formalised and regularised? How can a state that remains legally highly centralised, but contends with high levels of de facto decentralisation, function better?

The recent ‘National Conference for Partnership and Integration’, held in Aden in mid-June 2026, was a first step towards addressing these questions and launching a more constructive dialogue. It was organised by the Ministry of Local Administration with political backing from the President of the Presidential Leadership Council and the Prime Minister, with support from the Berghof Foundation and our local partner, the Political Development Forum.

The conference built on a survey examining key challenges and overlaps between the central and local levels in judicial and administrative affairs, development, resources and finance, as well as two preparatory workshops involving relevant line ministries and technical experts from the governorates. It aimed at identifying areas of existing agreement and outstanding differences. Participants recommended establishing a Higher Joint Coordination Council to continue the dialogue and develop an implementation framework that is realistic, sustainable, and workable for both sides.

The conference also highlighted that substantial disagreements around the relationship between the central and local authorities remain, with some ministries raising fundamental objections to the proposed reform agenda.

Coherent and effective governance is essential for peace

Agreement on revenues and other core issues will likely require more sustained dialogue between central and local authorities in the months and years ahead. All sides agree that such a process is necessary. However, it will require greater trust as well as recognition that decentralisation can ultimately benefit both the central government and local authorities. More coherent and effective governance, and a state capable of delivering basic services will also be needed to make any potential peace agreement stick.

After all, political discussions should remain focused on what matters most: easing citizens’ hardship and improving basic services. If the image of people taking their mattresses to the streets during Aden’s summer heat remains in the minds of decision-makers, it may help keep the process constructive and focused on tangible results.

item.title: How can Germany turn climate security commitments into action?
item.description:
Ahead of the Berlin Climate and Security Conference, we explore what Germany should do to support the climate, peace, and security agenda.

Climate stress and conflict increasingly overlap. Climate stress does not automatically cause conflict. But where it interacts with weak governance, inequality, and existing instability, it can increase pressure on resources and deepen grievances.

Germany is actively advocating for more support for the climate-security nexus. Yet multiple questions remain around how it can best leverage its position to further advance this cause.

This was the subject of a roundtable on “Climate, peace, and security: Advancing Germany’s policy response”, co-organised with the International Rescue Committee Germany, at our office in Berlin in July. Leading stakeholders from politics, business, academia, and civil society discussed how Germany can more effectively embed climate-related security risks into its national security architecture as well as facilitate access to climate finance for conflict-affected countries.

Berghof’s Executive Director Chris Coulter said Germany “needed to align what already exists far more effectively.” She stressed that climate change is not simply a technical issue: it shapes dialogue and mediation and can also provide an entry point for negotiations.

Climate change is not simply a technical issue: it shapes dialogue and mediation and can also provide an entry point for negotiations.Chris Coulter, Executive Director

Connecting climate, peace, and security

For years, climate change and security have been treated as separate issues. Security discussions still follow a conventional military approach. The effects of climate change are not only felt in fragile and conflict-affected countries though but also on supply chains, energy prices, and food security, which have political consequences for Germany and Europe. This framing does not dilute Germany's responsibility or solidarity with the countries hit hardest. However, it makes preventive action politically legible to a wider audience.

The time has come for political leaders to treat climate risk as a core national security priority. A positive sign in this direction was registered at this year’s London Climate Week where climate and nature were framed as systemic risks.

Where the gaps remain

If climate is genuinely treated as a security threat, funding should follow. However, global aid budgets are shrinking. Even if programmes stop running, affected communities still must keep living with the consequences and adapt accordingly. This is compounded by the fact that countries most affected by climate change receive the least funding.

The broader collective-action problem around climate finance also raises a hard question of fairness: who gets left behind? And how do they get brought back into the conversation?

Germany’s policy response

Germany is already playing a leading role in connecting climate, peace, and security. Together with the island state of Nauru, Germany established the UN Group of Friends on Climate and Security with now over 70 Member States. It placed climate security within its Foreign and National Security Strategy and has an advisory commission drawing on civil society expertise, among others. Ahead of this year’s Berlin Climate and Security Conference, the priority should now be to connect existing policies, institutions, and expertise and turn them into practical action.

  • First, Germany should strengthen coordination across foreign policy, development, humanitarian action, climate, and security. Ministries and agencies need shared analysis and clearer objectives, particularly in fragile and conflict-affected countries.

  • Second, Germany should make climate action more conflict sensitive, while ensuring that peacebuilding and humanitarian programmes account for climate pressures. It should also connect high-level diplomacy and mediation more effectively with local authorities and communities.

  • Third, Germany should keep conflict prevention and climate adaptation at the centre of its response. As aid budgets shrink, funding decisions should protect anticipatory action and support communities already facing the combined effects of climate shocks, conflict, and weak governance.

Germany cannot advance this agenda alone. It should continue to work with the United Kingdom, France, and other European partners on shared analysis and coordinated diplomacy. The United Kingdom's new taskforce on nature, climate, and security offers one possible route for exchange. Closer European cooperation would also give Germany’s agenda greater weight in international forums at a time of geopolitical fragmentation and tighter budgets.

Finally, climate security must move beyond its usual policy circles. The case for it needs to be presented in the rooms where decisions on defence, trade, energy and critical minerals are made. Germany has helped build the climate, peace, and security agenda. Its next challenge is to turn that leadership into a joined-up policy that prevents conflict, supports communities, and treats climate resilience as part of security preparedness.

item.title: From Maputo to the mountain
item.description:
This book details the journey of the Maputo Accord. Written by Mirko Manzoni and Neha Sanghrajka, who supported and facilitated the mediation and negotiation of the Accord, it traces step-by-step the painstaking efforts to build trust and confidence in often challenging circumstances, drawing on the authors’ own recollections of the mediation and subsequent efforts to implement the Accord. Insights from the mediators and others closely associated with the process bring to life Mozambique’s unique journey towards peace and reconciliation and the courage, perseverance and innovation of everyone involved.

Mirko Manzoni, Neha Sanghrajka

Download View online version

Reviews:

“The Maputo Accord stands as a beacon of hope, not only for Mozambique but for the entire region, reminding us of the profound power of dialogue and diplomacy in building lasting peace. Switzerland is honored to have been a steadfast partner to Mozambique on this transformative journey, and we hope that this legacy of collaboration will inspire others in their own efforts to build a sustainable and peaceful future. Our continued support reflects Switzerland’s commitment to fostering enduring peace and shared prosperity in Mozambique, grounded in trust and partnership.”
IGNAZIO CASSIS, Federal Councillor, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Swiss Confederation

“I have been honoured to play a role in the peace process in Mozambique. Working closely with Neha and Mirko I vividly recall those initial tense conversations as we sought to help build the foundations of the peace process. Over the past number of years I have continued to follow progress as the process stands out for me as uniquely innovative and collaborative. It brought together diverse perspectives and succeeded in fostering mutual understanding and reconciliation, through dialogue and trust-building. The firsthand account shared in this book captures the complexities of peacemaking, unpacking the delicate negotiations, power dynamics and challenges of building lasting peace in Mozambique. Having been engaged in the process on the ground, I am delighted to read the full account, told in a balanced and thoughtful way. I firmly believe the lessons from Mozambique’s peace process provide valuable contributions to the fields of conflict resolution and modern mediation, offering relevant and timely insights for other contexts.”
JONATHAN POWELL, National Security Adviser of the United Kingdom

“I have witnessed meaningful progress in Mozambique’s peace efforts and commend the ongoing commitment to dialogue as a key tool for sustaining peace and advancing national reconciliation. Mozambique’s experience offers a compelling example of how African solutions can address African challenges and create sustainable pathways to peace. This way Silencing the Guns becomes more than an aspiration but a necessity for a prosperous Mozambique.”
DR. MOHAMED IBN CHAMBAS, African Union High Representative for Silencing the Guns

item.title: Perspectives for a renewed social contract in Lebanon
item.description:
Lebanon has faced a succession of overlapping crises—including the 2019 financial collapse, the Beirut port explosion, institutional paralysis, recurring Israeli aggressions, and ongoing political and regional instability—that have profoundly reshaped state–citizen relations and intensified long-standing governance challenges. Against this backdrop, Westminster Foundation for Democracy, and the Berghof Foundation conducted research from March–December 2025 to examine how diverse groups of Lebanese citizens understand the current social contract, their priorities for a renewed and inclusive one, and the barriers and opportunities for achieving it.

Lara Azzam, Mohammad Al Mishlawi, Jana Sleem

item.title: Transformative transitional justice and climate action
item.description:
In the face of rapidly escalating but unevenly distributed harms, global climate governance is struggling to prevent catastrophic warming while addressing growing demands for climate justice. This paper proposes transformative transitional justice as a lens through which to identify two sources of climate justice action: elements of justice latent within climate policy architectures, and community justice actions too often overlooked by formal institutions. It identifies ways to connect these institutional and community-level elements into a broader, multi-level justice ecosystem.

Jasmina Brankovic, Samuel Sontag

Download

In the first part, the paper identifies several entry points within the global climate framework to advance climate justice. The second part provides insights into key findings from participatory research into community-led climate actions in Malawi and the Philippines – highlighting that communities are already pursuing climate justice actions that align with transformative transitional justice principles – actions that institutional actors systematically fail to identify and acknowledge. The research shows the need for integrating communities’ braided experience of harm and articulations of justice with the institutional infrastructure of the global climate regime into a justice ecosystem that allows for more transformative climate justice.

item.title: After the peace process, the mountains are burning
item.description:
This paper explores the intersection of climate justice and transitional justice through the case study of community-level climate initiatives in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), Philippines. It identifies community-led climate actions that fuse transitional justice elements of truth-telling, reparative agency, and guarantees of non-recurrence in ways that challenge institutional silos between post-conflict and environmental governance. The findings demonstrate that addressing climate disasters in the BARMM is inseparable from resolving the historical land-based injustices and colonial displacement that created communal vulnerability. The study concludes that institutional frameworks must recognise and support community-led climate justice rather than displacing local agency with top-down technical solutions, and identifies the Bangsamoro Transitional Justice and Reconciliation Act of 2025 as a critical institutional opening for this integration.

Samuel Sontag, Reemar Alonsagay

item.title: Local transitional justice practices for climate justice
item.description:
This paper explores the intersection of climate justice and transitional justice through the case study of community-level engagements with climate change in the rural area of Nkhulambe, Malawi. It shows that residents have developed their own climate responses that tackle more fully the manifold climate harms they have experienced than top-down climate responses to date. These community-led measures address climate harms which occurred in the past, while building solidarity in the present, in order to prevent and reduce the harms of future climate events, as such they can be understood as climate-focused transformative transitional justice in practice. Moreover, they have the potential to complement and strengthen top-down national and international efforts, making them more inclusive and responsive to communities affected by climate harms, as well as opening the door to more equitable climate action.

Jasmina Brankovic

item.title: Peace Mediation and Transitional Justice
item.description:
The 2023 EEAS Peace Mediation Guidelines highlight the importance for mediators to engage with transitional justice frameworks. Experience shows that when transitional justice is sidelined as a purely post‑conflict issue, peace agreements often lack legitimacy and public acceptance. Sustainable peace therefore depends on addressing the legacy of past violence through appropriate transitional justice approaches.

This paper argues that transitional justice encompasses a wide range of judicial and non‑judicial mechanisms that, if carefully sequenced and contextually adapted, can be constructively integrated into peace mediation.

Luxshi Vimalarajah, Charlotte Hamm

item.title: Mapping Service Provision at the Local Level in Yemen
item.description:
This study maps the provision of electricity, water and cleanliness services in five Yemeni cities. It highlights how the war has reshaped local systems, where they have proven resilient, and what is needed to restore a minimum functioning public service. It argues for addressing security and governance challenges affecting service provision, rebuilding a basic social contract with citizens, and foregrounding long-term sustainability against the temptation of quick fixes when investing into public service infrastructure and equipment.

Dr. Ahmed Almaweri
